surface/mcp/instructions.why: The MCP instructions lead with the cheap way to write cases (coverage, case_new, map_plan, then driving) and with case_impact after a code change; a trial agent never found those tools from the old text. The FastSim paragraph says a FastSim bundle is a release bundle, so the app must call qa.register outside if (__DEV__); a trial agent registered its commands behind __DEV__ and they were missing on FastSim. It also says case_run and fastsim_start bundle a stale FastSim bundle again (with the server's environment) or refuse the run, so an agent never reports on old code. It also places crawl in that cheap path, before driving by hand, and says the route map rebuilds itself and learns from every press. The instructions tell an agent to keep the way case_new offers and to put steps several cases open with in a macro, and that verbose shows a failed case whole. Where to run now says to write a case where it is cheapest and most reliable (FastSim when the organization has it, else headless; a Simulator or emulator when the case needs a device), and that a case is done when it passes on every available target, checked with one case_run with on: all. The instructions say case_run with out writes report.html to open offline, and that film is taken on FastSim, a Simulator or an emulator. The instructions were cut to the essentials (what Lynkeus is, status and init, the cheap path, case_impact, the device rule, native mocks are the person's call, FastSim refusals) and point at the guide tool; the rest (FastSim setup, sharing a run, evidence, teardown and sections, long suites, launch facts, mocks) moved to the guide topics and the Lynkeus skill, which cost nothing until read. They were re-read on every call of a session. A case is done when case_run with on: targets passes on the project's cases.targets, not on every available target: a trial agent ran iOS, Android and headless for every case; with none declared the agent asks the person. The guide paragraph says a topic lists its sections and a topic and section answer one. It says to read a section when the task reaches it, not up front: a trial agent read four whole topics up front and paid for them again on about 215 later calls. A last paragraph says routine work (setup, status, suites, evidence) runs well on a smaller model or lower effort while writing and debugging cases gains from a stronger one, and names the lynkeus-setup and lynkeus-runner subagents for clients that have subagents; Lynkeus suggests, the person decides. The instructions lead with the one-call jobs (setup, case_run with on: targets and brief, evidence) over driving builds, Metro and devices through the shell, say to open a job's log files only when its answer points at one, and that a client that can run a task in a separate context should hand it those jobs and keep only their summaries; the paragraph naming one client's subagents is gone. The device rule says Lynkeus boots only a device the project names, and setup says when it does.

surface/commands.why: fastsim start and fastsim stop: a FastSim host for a session or an MCP server to explore on. report html writes a run folder as an offline HTML page. guide serves the Lynkeus skill's topics one at a time; skill install installs or updates the skill in .claude/skills/lynkeus. setup connects an app in one call (init, the device, Metro, the development build, launch, attach, status) and evidence runs cases with frames, film and report.html and answers a short summary: an agent spent dozens of shell calls on what setup does.

surface/help/fastsim start.why: new command: starts a FastSim host on the session's driver port. A bundle older than the app's code is bundled again first (or the start is refused with the command), instead of only a warning.

surface/help/fastsim stop.why: new command: stops the host fastsim start started

surface/mcp/full.why: fastsim_start and fastsim_stop are served over MCP. report_html is served over MCP. guide is served over MCP; init takes no_skill. setup and evidence are served over MCP; case_run takes brief.

surface/mcp/tool/fastsim_start.why: new tool: explore the app on a FastSim host. A bundle older than the app's code is bundled again first (or the start is refused with the command), instead of only a warning.

surface/mcp/tool/fastsim_stop.why: new tool: stops the host fastsim_start started

surface/usage.why: the usage lists fastsim start and fastsim stop os language also takes --app. case run lists --verbose. os language and its siblings also take --device, and os language works on Android (API 33+). case run takes --on (simulator, fastsim, headless or all) to run the same cases on several targets at once, one line per case per target, and --bundle to name the FastSim bundle it uses; a run without --on is unchanged. The usage lists report html. The usage lists guide and skill install, and init's --no-skill. The usage lists map ci's --cases. The usage lists guide [topic] [section]. The usage says skill install also installs the Claude Code subagents in .claude/agents. init's --no-skill help mentions the subagents. The usage lists setup, evidence and case run's --brief. The usage lists report html --embed-film. The usage lists why --on. case run and evidence take --budget (1500 s by default over MCP, so one call ends before a client gives up on it; in trial 7 a run went silent for 30 minutes and outlived the call by two hours), and a step past its timeoutMs plus 30 s, or 180 s without one, fails as stuck.

report/answer.why: A failed case's summary now opens with the failing step's own error (— failed at: <step>), which it used to leave out when the evidence explained nothing. A failed case in the summary names its step's place (failed at step 2 of 3) without a second result line, its screen is cut to what a check can name and only requests worth a look are listed (verbose keeps it all); each step and case now carry the screens the run went through. On a phone, a case reads the screen once more before its first step (to relaunch an app covered by a view it did not draw), which moves the virtual clock by a millisecond. A run with --out ends with the path of the report.html it wrote beside the run. Each step carries its phases (marks, target, action, settle, wait, look, events: where its ms went, timed where the runner already waits) in the case's report and cases.jsonl; timing them adds no message but reads the virtual clock in a few more places. A press with its own timeoutMs is held to it in every wait for its target (the wait for it to be listed, the scrolls, the wait for it to be enabled and still), so a missing target fails at its timeout instead of up to 15 s later: the failure's screen is read earlier (a lower commit) and the virtual clock moves less.

surface/help/case stop.why: case stop is new: it stops a case run that is going, from a terminal or over MCP (case_stop).

surface/mcp/tool/case_stop.why: case_stop is a new MCP tool, so a model can stop a case_run its client moved to the background.

wire/press-by-number.why: A failed case reads its reasons from the trace since the case's first step (trace since), not the whole trace, so an older failure is not given as its cause. A target written as a bare number is an index: app.press: 2 presses element 2 instead of failing with "Cannot use 'in' operator". Each step carries its phases (marks, target, action, settle, wait, look, events: where its ms went, timed where the runner already waits) in the case's report and cases.jsonl; timing them adds no message but reads the virtual clock in a few more places.

surface/help/case run.why: --jobs and --host-command no longer need --ports: free driver ports are picked when none are given, as the FastSim guide promised. case run takes --verbose: without it a failed case's screen is cut to what a check can name, only requests that failed or were mocked are listed and a notice the last run gave is not repeated; --seen defaults to .lynkeus/seen and keeps the screen after each step. case run takes --on (simulator, fastsim, headless or all) to run the same cases on several targets at once, one line per case per target, and --bundle to name the FastSim bundle it uses; a run without --on is unchanged. --video films on a Simulator (simctl io recordVideo) and an emulator (adb shell screenrecord) too, not only on a host that films. --on takes ios and android, the iOS Simulator's app and the Android emulator's side by side on the driver port, each on its own connection; all is ios, android, fastsim and headless, and simulator stays whichever device app is attached. `--on targets` runs each case on its declared targets (cases.targets, or its own targets: frontmatter) and a declared target missing here makes the check incomplete; FastSim is named per platform (fastsim:ios, fastsim:android), and `all` takes both. case run --host and case here --host start their headless host on a free driver port of its own: on the configured port it met a device app attached there and the run drove both (a trial saw the emulator's screens and another case's mocks). case run takes --brief: with --on, only the cases that did not pass, each target's count and notes cut to a line. Every case on FastSim gets a host of its own (--on fastsim:*, ci, a fastsim-run --host-command, --keep-hosts or not): a kept FastSim host was never reset, and in trial 7 nine of ten cases started signed in from the first; --host-timeout now also bounds a host started for one case. case run and evidence take --budget (1500 s by default over MCP, so one call ends before a client gives up on it; in trial 7 a run went silent for 30 minutes and outlived the call by two hours), and a step past its timeoutMs plus 30 s, or 180 s without one, fails as stuck.

surface/mcp/tool/case_run.why: --jobs and --host-command no longer need --ports: free driver ports are picked when none are given, as the FastSim guide promised. case run takes --verbose: without it a failed case's screen is cut to what a check can name, only requests that failed or were mocked are listed and a notice the last run gave is not repeated; --seen defaults to .lynkeus/seen and keeps the screen after each step. case run takes --on (simulator, fastsim, headless or all) to run the same cases on several targets at once, one line per case per target, and --bundle to name the FastSim bundle it uses; a run without --on is unchanged. --host with --jobs starts one headless host per job on that job's port (one host on the configured port attached to no job's driver). A headless host that serves several cases is reset before each case after its first (a shared host leaked state from case to case). Its description says a member read and never called that the library's TurboModule spec declares a method is left out of the native values notice. --on takes ios and android, the iOS Simulator's app and the Android emulator's side by side on the driver port, each on its own connection; all is ios, android, fastsim and headless, and simulator stays whichever device app is attached. `on: targets` runs each case on its declared targets (cases.targets, or its own targets: frontmatter) and a declared target missing here makes the check incomplete; FastSim is named per platform (fastsim:ios, fastsim:android). The description now says the seed does not reach the app on an attached simulator or emulator (only the cases' {{random.*}}), as run.json and the determinism guide say; it said only the seed applied there. case run --host and case here --host start their headless host on a free driver port of its own: on the configured port it met a device app attached there and the run drove both (a trial saw the emulator's screens and another case's mocks). case_run over MCP takes frames, settle and still, which the determinism guide recommends for frames compared pixel for pixel. case_run takes brief (with on: only the cases that did not pass, each target's count, notes cut to a line). Its details point at the guide for launch facts and native values instead of repeating them on every turn. Every case on FastSim gets a host of its own (--on fastsim:*, ci, a fastsim-run --host-command, --keep-hosts or not): a kept FastSim host was never reset, and in trial 7 nine of ten cases started signed in from the first; --host-timeout now also bounds a host started for one case. case run and evidence take --budget (1500 s by default over MCP, so one call ends before a client gives up on it; in trial 7 a run went silent for 30 minutes and outlived the call by two hours), and a step past its timeoutMs plus 30 s, or 180 s without one, fails as stuck.

Each step carries its phases (marks, target, action, settle, wait, look, events: where its ms went, timed where the runner already waits) in the case's report and cases.jsonl; timing them adds no message but reads the virtual clock in a few more places. On a host that is not a device (hello native false: the headless host), a press by testId no longer waits a quiet window (idle 50 ms) to read its target twice alike, since such a host has no transition to wait out and the agent's press waits for the target to hold still; and app.type no longer waits for the app to go quiet (idle 100 ms) after its field is listed. A trial measured headless presses at about 520 ms, most of it fixed waits.

surface/help/headless init.why: headless init no longer writes a local-backend guard: the entry runs the app's own entry and the host's network fence keeps the app off non-local hosts, so the summary says what it writes now.

surface/mcp/tool/headless_init.why: headless init no longer writes a local-backend guard: the entry runs the app's own entry and the host's network fence keeps the app off non-local hosts, so the summary says what it writes now.

surface/help/map build.why: map build's help says it is rarely needed by hand now: every command that reads the graph rebuilds it when it is missing or older than the source it was read from.

surface/help/crawl.why: crawl is served over MCP by default, bounded to one level and 12 presses per call unless the call asks for more, and answers with a short summary (screens, new edges, problems): an agent learns the app's ways in one call instead of pressing by hand. A press that sends the app to the background (a link opened in the browser) is a transition outside the app: reported with what it opened, never repeated, and the app is brought back to the front.

surface/help/case coverage.why: case coverage reads the screens case run now keeps by default, and hints at a macro for steps three or more cases open with. A screen counts as covered when a macro the case calls goes to it, waits for it or checks it, so a CI checkout without .lynkeus/seen still covers screens reached only inside macros (a trial missed showroom-demos).

surface/help/case impact.why: case run keeps the screens of passing cases in .lynkeus/seen without --seen now, so the flag's help no longer points at case run --seen. A change to a string table (an object literal of strings, such as the app’s translations) counts only for the files that name its changed keys and the cases that check a changed text, unless a changed key is named nowhere by its whole key. A file whose change is only testIDs or accessibility labels (or comments and formatting) reaches no screen, only the cases that name a changed testID or label.

surface/help/case new.why: case new offers the way an existing case takes to the screen (from the steps case run now keeps in .lynkeus/seen by default), and case coverage names steps three or more cases open with, as a macro to declare. case new begins, without --from or cases.start, at the screen the attached app shows or the first screen declared, and names the fixtures in one comment (none for the example server case init writes). Without --from, a start with no known way gives way to cases.start, then the first declared screen (a trial began on DemoShowroom and found no way to About that map plan knew from Welcome); a draft for a screen no case reaches lists what its source and runs know is on it.

report/file/run.json.why: An attached simulator or emulator lists seed under launch.unsupported: the seed makes the cases' {{random.*}} repeatable, but the app's Math.random is its own, and a trial read the old manifest as the app being seeded.

surface/help/map ci.why: map ci checks 4 imports away by default, as case impact and ci --affected do, so the PR comment and the affected cases agree; it used 2. map ci --cases adds a job running lynkeus ci --affected on the project's CI targets (cases.targets), opt-in because it needs the app's backend and, for FastSim, a key in the CI secrets; without it, map ci says what --cases would add.

surface/help/report html.why: report html is new: it writes a run folder as one HTML page to open offline (no reports service). --embed no longer inlines the film (it stays a file beside the page); --embed-film does.

surface/mcp/tool/report_html.why: report_html is new: it writes report.html into a run folder, to open offline. embed no longer inlines the film; embedFilm does.

report/files.why: A run with --out writes report.html beside run.json, a page to open offline.

surface/help/guide.why: guide is new: the Lynkeus skill's topics (cases, targets, evidence, ci, determinism, troubleshooting) one at a time, for clients without skills. guide takes an optional section after the topic: a topic alone lists its sections one line each, a topic and section answer that section only, so an agent reads a few hundred bytes instead of a whole topic it then pays for on every later call.

surface/help/skill install.why: skill install is new: installs or updates the Lynkeus skill in .claude/skills/lynkeus, leaving an edited one alone unless --force. Its details say the same sections are served by guide. skill install also installs the Claude Code subagents lynkeus-setup and lynkeus-runner in .claude/agents (on a cheaper model, Lynkeus tools only), each protected from overwriting like the skill.

surface/help/init.why: init also installs the Lynkeus skill (how to write, run and debug cases, read by clients that load Agent Skills) in .claude/skills/lynkeus and says so; --no-skill leaves it out, and a skill the person edited is never overwritten. --no-skill can also be set with LYNKEUS_NO_SKILL=1. init's --no-skill help says it leaves the Claude Code subagents out too.

surface/mcp/tool/guide.why: guide is a core MCP tool: one topic of the Lynkeus skill per call, with the topics as an enum. guide takes an optional section (a plain string, not an enum, to keep the schema small): a topic alone lists its sections, a topic and section answer that section only.

surface/help/nav.why: nav reaches a screen inside a nested navigator through its parents (from the path a run saw or the route graph), and its help says so, with the screen it lands on and via.

surface/help/ci.why: With cases.targets declared, lynkeus ci runs each case on its declared targets a CI job can start (headless, fastsim:ios, fastsim:android), one after another, lists the device ones as not run, and fails as incomplete when a declared FastSim target cannot start.

surface/help/case here.why: case run --host and case here --host start their headless host on a free driver port of its own: on the configured port it met a device app attached there and the run drove both (a trial saw the emulator's screens and another case's mocks).

surface/mcp/tool/case_here.why: case run --host and case here --host start their headless host on a free driver port of its own: on the configured port it met a device app attached there and the run drove both (a trial saw the emulator's screens and another case's mocks).

surface/help/fastsim install.why: fastsim install says that, without a terminal, a missing or expired sign-in exits 2 with a first line saying signing in is a step only the person can do (lynkeus login): in a trial an agent over MCP had only the service's invalid_grant to go by.

report/file/missing.2/01-app-press-incre.why: A press with its own timeoutMs is held to it in every wait for its target (the wait for it to be listed, the scrolls, the wait for it to be enabled and still), so a missing target fails at its timeout instead of up to 15 s later: the failure's screen is read earlier (a lower commit) and the virtual clock moves less.

report/file/missing.2/02-app-press-targe.why: A press with its own timeoutMs is held to it in every wait for its target (the wait for it to be listed, the scrolls, the wait for it to be enabled and still), so a missing target fails at its timeout instead of up to 15 s later: the failure's screen is read earlier (a lower commit) and the virtual clock moves less.

report/file/missing/02-app-press-target-.why: A press with its own timeoutMs is held to it in every wait for its target (the wait for it to be listed, the scrolls, the wait for it to be enabled and still), so a missing target fails at its timeout instead of up to 15 s later: the failure's screen is read earlier (a lower commit) and the virtual clock moves less.

surface/help/evidence.why: new command: evidence runs cases with frames, film and report.html and answers only the report path, each case per target and the frames that look wrong. case run and evidence take --budget (1500 s by default over MCP, so one call ends before a client gives up on it; in trial 7 a run went silent for 30 minutes and outlived the call by two hours), and a step past its timeoutMs plus 30 s, or 180 s without one, fails as stuck.

surface/help/setup.why: new command: setup connects an app in one call (init, the device, Metro, the project's own development build, launch, attach, status), safe to run again, with logs in .lynkeus/runs/setup.

surface/mcp/tool/evidence.why: new tool: evidence, the evidence run as one call with a short answer, so a session does not carry a whole run's output. case run and evidence take --budget (1500 s by default over MCP, so one call ends before a client gives up on it; in trial 7 a run went silent for 30 minutes and outlived the call by two hours), and a step past its timeoutMs plus 30 s, or 180 s without one, fails as stuck.

surface/mcp/tool/setup.why: new tool: setup, connecting an app as one call with a short answer and MCP progress, instead of 36 shell calls for builds, Metro and devices in a trial session.

surface/help/why.why: why takes --on <platform>: when two apps share the port it explains the lane of the attached app (or the one named), never the other lane's case.

surface/mcp/tool/why.why: why takes on (ios or android): the lane to explain when two apps share the port.
